# A uniform pyramid section-centroid barrier in every dimension

This is a new bounded uniform-body statement. It classifies every centroidal section of a nonsimplex family and proves its balanced weighted stationary-cap inequality with the exact value 1/2. It does not prove the general weighted stationary-section conjecture or OC.

The archived `candidate 95f421513ee961a1` constructs some oblique centroidal sections of nonsymmetric cones, but does not give this classification. The rank-two theorem is also already proved in the archive; the present input is instead an all-direction geometric exclusion for a specified uniform body. The classification ultimately makes its balanced menus decomposable, a limitation retained below.

## 1. Statement

Let d>=2, let D be ANY centrally symmetric convex body in R^(d−1), centered at zero, and fix 0<H<=d−1. In R^(d−1) times R set

    K=conv(D times {−1}, {(0,H)}).

The point zero is interior to K. Then:

* If 0<H<d−1, the ONLY through-zero hyperplane whose section has centroid zero is the horizontal plane z=0.
* If H=d−1, the through-zero sections with centroid zero are exactly the horizontal section and all vertical sections u.X=0.
* More precisely, every nonhorizontal, nonvertical section through zero has STRICTLY NEGATIVE mean z-coordinate.

Consequently let u_i be any finite collection of unit inward cap normals whose sections K intersect u_i-perp have centroid zero. Let S_i be their (d−1)-areas and let theta_i>=0, sum theta_i=1, satisfy

    sum_i theta_i S_i u_i=0.

For the associated closed halfspaces H_i={u_i.x>=0},

    sum_i theta_i |K intersect H_i|=|K|/2.                  (1)

In particular the desired lower bound Gamma_d|K| holds strictly. No smoothness, polytope structure or symmetry of the whole pyramid is assumed. D can be a ball, an arbitrary centrally symmetric polytope, or a nonsmooth centrally symmetric body.

## 2. An elementary signed-integral lemma

For H>0 and R>0 put

    J_(d,H)(R)=integral_(-R)^min(R,1) q/(H+1−q)^(d+1) dq.

If 0<H<=d−1, then J_(d,H)(R)>0 for EVERY R>0.

For R<=1 pair q and −q. The integral becomes

    integral_0^R q[(H+1−q)^(−d−1)
                         −(H+1+q)^(−d−1)]dq>0.

For R>=1, direct integration gives

    integral_(-infinity)^1 q/(H+1−q)^(d+1)dq
       =(d−1−H)/[d(d−1)H^d]>=0.                          (2)

The omitted tail (−infinity,−R) has a strictly negative integral. Removing it makes the integral strictly positive. The integral at infinity is finite for d>=2, and the denominator at the upper endpoint is H>0. These arguments include R=1 without a limiting convention.

It follows that if f is a nonzero compactly supported even density, nonincreasing on the positive halfline, positive near zero, then

    integral_(q<=1) q f(q)/(H+1−q)^(d+1)dq>0.              (3)

Indeed its layer-cake superlevel sets are symmetric intervals, up to null endpoints. Apply the preceding strict inequality to each positive-length interval. Fubini is legitimate for this signed integrand: f has bounded compact support and the denominator on q<=1 is at least H. No logconcavity approximation is used.

## 3. Actual oblique section and its first moment

Write points of the pyramid as

    X=r b,        z=H−(H+1)r,        b in D, 0<=r<=1.

A through-zero nonvertical plane is z=−a.X. If a is nonzero, its actual section is parameterized exactly by

    b in D_a=D intersect {a.b<=1},
    r=H/(H+1−a.b),
    X=H b/(H+1−a.b).                                    (4)

The denominator is at least H on D_a. The apex is not on the plane, so no point of the section is lost by this parametrization. Its graph factor for section area is sqrt(1+|a|^2). The projective map in (4), in dimension d−1, has Jacobian

    H^(d−1)(H+1)/(H+1−a.b)^d.                            (5)

This follows by the matrix determinant lemma, or directly by differentiating the scalar denominator. The map is one-to-one: its explicit inverse is b=(H+1)X/(H+a.X), whose denominator on the image is positive. Thus the usual change of variables applies.

Combining (4) and (5), the section first moment of a.X has the sign of

    integral_(D_a) (a.b)/(H+1−a.b)^(d+1) db.               (6)

The omitted factor is the strictly positive number sqrt(1+|a|^2) H^d(H+1).

The pushforward density f(q) of uniform base volume under q=a.b is even, compactly supported, and nonincreasing for q>=0. For d=2 this density is constant on a symmetric interval. For d>2, evenness follows from D=−D, and section Brunn–Minkowski gives the claimed monotonicity: a section at a height between −t and t contains a Minkowski combination of the equal-volume sections at those two heights. The central section has positive measure, so f is positive near zero.

Equation (3) therefore makes (6) strictly positive. On the section z=−a.X, its mean z-coordinate is strictly negative. In particular its centroid is not zero. This proof permits sections meeting base facets or nonsmooth edges: the parameter boundary a.b=1 has zero (d−1)-dimensional base volume, and all denominators in the actual interior remain positive.

## 4. Horizontal and vertical sections

The horizontal section z=0 is a positive homothetic copy [H/(H+1)]D. Its centroid is zero.

A vertical section u.X=0 is a (d−1)-dimensional pyramid with base D intersect u-perp at height −1 and apex at height H. Its base centroid is zero by central symmetry, so its section centroid has vertical coordinate

    [H−(d−1)]/d.                                         (7)

For d=2 this is simply the midpoint of the vertical interval. Thus a vertical section is centroidal precisely when H=d−1. Along with Section 3 this proves the complete classification.

The horizontal cap facing the apex has volume fraction

    p=[H/(H+1)]^d,

and the opposite cap has fraction 1−p. Every vertical cap has fraction 1/2, because reflection (X,z)→(−X,z) preserves K and exchanges its two sides. Closed cutting hyperplanes have zero d-volume.

## 5. Exact balanced average and scope

For H<d−1, every allowed normal is one of the two horizontal unit normals. Their common section area is S>0. Coarea-weighted balance forces their total weights equal, proving (1).

For H=d−1, collect the total weights theta_+,theta_- of the two horizontal orientations and theta_v of all vertical normals. The vertical coordinate of the balance still forces theta_+=theta_-, since all vertical normals have zero last coordinate and both horizontal sections have the same area S. Therefore

    theta_+ p+theta_-(1−p)+theta_v/2
       =(theta_++theta_-+theta_v)/2=1/2.

This includes arbitrarily many sections and zero weights. Full-rank balanced menus are possible when H=d−1, but their normal balance necessarily splits between the horizontal line and the vertical subspace. The theorem does NOT exclude or resolve irreducible full-rank stationary circuits in a general body.

The apex-facing stationary cap can be much smaller than Gamma_d: as H tends to zero its fraction tends to zero. The result comes from actual uniform section geometry plus balance, not an assertion that every stationary section is individually deep. The nonuniform zonoid counterexample does not satisfy the monotone uniform-base section structure used in (3)–(6).
